preamble: The voiceless velar fricative [x] fronts to the voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ] before high front vowels and glides, a palatalization that moves the constriction from the velum to the prepalatal region. The best-known case is northern Sinitic, where the Middle Chinese 曉 initial stays [x] before back vowels but became [ɕ] before /i y/ in Mandarin, Jin and Xiang alike. Slavic shows the same change in its second palatalization, where *x before front vowels became *ś, preserved as ś [ɕ] in Polish.

examples.note: Over the last few centuries the velar initials palatalized before [i] and [y], merging with the dental sibilants into the [tɕ tɕʰ ɕ] series spelled ⟨j q x⟩ in Pinyin. The same 曉 initial stays [x] before back vowels: 海 hǎi /xaɪ̯²¹⁴/ 'sea' versus 希 xī /ɕi⁵⁵/ 'hope'.
Taiyuan keeps [x] before non-front vowels (海 /xai⁵³/ 'sea') but has [ɕ] before /i/.
Changsha likewise contrasts 海 /xai̯⁴¹/ 'sea' with palatalized 希 /ɕi³³/.

In the Slavic second palatalization *x before front vowels (here *-i < *-oi) became *ś; Polish keeps ś [ɕ], while East and South Slavic have s and Czech š. The singular Włoch preserves the unpalatalized [x].

sources: Norman, J. (1988). Chinese. Cambridge University Press.
Baxter, W. H. (1992). A Handbook of Old Chinese Phonology. Mouton de Gruyter.
